Everything begins by thinning at the edges.

It does not announce itself with thunder or the tearing of skies. There are no trumpets, no fissures opening in the asphalt to swallow the municipal buildings or the rows of modest brick houses. Instead, a color loses its courage on a Tuesday afternoon. The blue of an enamel kettle on the back burner of a stove becomes slightly less obstinate about being blue; by Thursday, it is the color of pond water seen through fog; by the following month, you look at the stove and remember only that something once kept the tea warm, though you cannot quite recall its shape.

My father called this the *attrition of the uncherished*. He was a binder of ledgers, a man who spent forty years with his thumbs stained the color of walnut husks from bone-folding glue and calfskin. He believed that the universe was held together not by gravity, which he considered a blunt and unimaginative force, but by the friction of human attention.

"If you don't look at a fence post for thirty years," he told me once, trimming the uneven deckle of an octavo volume with a curved steel blade, "it doesn't rot. It simply loses the habit of standing there. It wanders off into the potential."

I was nine years old, and I spent the rest of that summer staring relentlessly at the doorknobs of our house, terrified that if I blinked for too long, our bedrooms would spill out into the blank, untended sky.

***

Now, fifty years later, I live alone in a house that smells of sea salt and dried bay leaves, situated on a spit of land that the local maps have drawn three different ways in my lifetime. None of the maps are incorrect; the coast is merely fickle. It retracts when the wind comes out of the northeast, and it stretches out like a cat waking on a warm flagstone when the low-pressure systems drift in from the islands.

Every morning, before the kettle whistles, I walk the perimeter of the garden and take inventory.

There is the dry-stone wall, built by a stonemason whose name has already vanished from the parish register. The stones are basalt, dark and pockmarked like the crust of overbaked bread. In the crevices, sea-campion grows in stubborn little tufts, white petals trembling against the salt spray. I touch each capping stone with the flat of my palm. *One, two, three, four.* I give them their weight back. I remind them of down-ness.

There is the pear tree, which has not borne fruit since the year of the frost, but which still insists on producing twelve dozen perfect, glossy leaves each May. I run two fingers down the furrowed bark of its lowest bough. *You are wood,* I tell it silently. *You have roots that go down into the black shale beneath the topsoil. You are not an idea.*

People believe that forgetting is a passive act—a slow draining of water from a cracked cistern. They are mistaken. Forgetting is an appetite. It is an enormous, patient mouth that lives just behind the scenery, waiting for an actor to miss a cue, waiting for a painter to put down her brush and turn her back on the canvas.

If you leave a room empty for an hour, it remains a room. If you leave it empty for twenty years, the walls begin to doubt the floor. The corners lose their right angles. The dust does not settle upon the surfaces; the surfaces turn into dust because they no longer have any reason to maintain the pretense of being a table, a mantle, a chair.

***

In the village three miles south, they have built a road of glass and asphalt that bypasses the old coach road entirely. The lorries move across it with the sound of torn silk, carrying plastic crates of milk, frozen cod, prefabricated timber, and television screens flat as pond ice. The drivers do not look at the fields they bisect. They cannot; to look at seventy miles an hour is to invite catastrophe.

As a consequence, the fields between the new highway and the sea are becoming vague.

Last week I walked out into the middle of what used to be the Miller’s Acre—a piece of common pasture that had fed five generations of dairy cattle. I stood in the center of it under an overcast sky that had neither sun nor rain in it, just a flat, milky luminescence that cast no shadows.

The grass was there, but when I knelt and pressed my hand against the turf, there was no resistance. It was like resting one’s fingers on the surface of a very deep, cold pool. The blades gave way without bending; the earth did not smell of iron or worms or decay. It smelled of nothing at all—a clean, terrifying blankness, like the inside of a new cardboard box before anything has ever been packed into it.

"Hold on," I whispered to the sod. "Hold on, damn you."

I took a copper coin from my coat pocket—an old penny from 1936, thick and heavy, with the profile of an empire’s ghost stamped into its face—and I pushed it into the soil with my thumb. I pushed it until it disappeared beneath the mossy root-tangle. I gave the ground something dense to hold, an anchor of worked metal, an artifact of somebody’s labor, an alloy of copper and time.

For a moment, the ground shuddered. A faint fragrance rose—damp humus, wild mint, wet slate. The world remembered itself for fifty yards in every direction. The grass stiffened against the hem of my trousers. A crow, startled into existence by the sudden solidity of an ash branch overhead, shook its feathers, gave a harsh, indignant croak, and beat its way toward the headland.

***

We are losing the nouns. That is the truth of it.

We have plenty of verbs—*moving, streaming, accelerating, updating, consuming, deleting*—but the nouns are going soft around the middle. We have forgotten what an auger feels like in the palm of a hand on a freezing November morning; we have forgotten the specific, resinous tang of pitch used to caulk the bottom of an oak dinghy; we have forgotten the difference between the sound of rain on slate and the sound of rain on lead.

When everything is converted into light on a screen, everything becomes equally weightless. A photograph of your mother’s wedding carries the same physical presence as a photograph of a stranger’s breakfast: five volts of illumination across three square inches of glass. Neither has a back. Neither can be creased, or stained with butter, or kept in the bottom of a cedar chest until it smells of linen and winter.

When my time comes, I know how it will happen.

I will not fall ill, and my heart will not burst like an overfilled bladder. I will simply look at my hand one morning while the kettle boils, and I will notice that the veins are no longer blue, but grey; that the skin is translucent as tracing paper; that the kitchen table behind my knuckles is entirely visible.

I will feel no pain. I will only feel a profound, light-headed relief, like a swimmer who has finally decided to stop fighting the long, slow drift of the tide.

Until then, there are still the capping stones. There is still the pear tree with its twelve dozen leaves. There is still the brass latch on the front gate, which sticks if you do not lift it slightly from below, and which demands, every single afternoon, that you remember it was made by a man who had two thumbs, three daughters, and a furnace full of coke.

I walk out onto the porch. The wind has turned. The salt is thick upon the glass.

I put my hands against the railing, grip the damp cedar with all the strength left in my fingers, and push downward until I am certain that the earth is beneath me, and that I am upon the earth.
